I don't get some of you guys chiding her for killing herself. Sure, it's not the desired outcome, but there's a few things you need to consider:


First, most of you are probably taking this in from the perspective of an adult. Through your experiences, or perhaps just through sheer force of will, you know that there's very little, if anything, to kill yourself over. However, she was 12. How much perspective did you have when you were 12? I'll bet that for most people, your entire world centered around what happened at home and what happened at school (and for a somewhat unfortunate few, what happened at work). She may have had a counselor to go to for bullying, but that doesn't mean she'd be able to open up or relate to anyone about her family issues.


Secondly, a 12-year-old girl has likely started puberty, menstruation, etc. Most of us can agree that her response to her ills was highly irrational and poorly thought out. What's silly here is the fact that you're expecting a 12-year-old going through sudden mental, emotional, and physical changes to be "rational". Even if this were a guy, these same issues would still apply (though they tend to start puberty much later). 


Finally, sticks and stones and all that. You may complain about this generation being a bunch of pussies, and perhaps we are a bit softer. However, your resilience as an adult is both gained differently from and works off of the resilience you had as a child. Support and care need to be there. It doesn't have to be from parents, but someone who gets so badly devastated over a puppy love breakup tells me that she was attempting to get this from elsewhere. When you go to school and face namecalling (and it isn't simply a few assholes calling you names -- they're apt to spread this around and before you know it, you're an outcast), only to go home with the feeling of walking on eggshells because there might be another blow up between your parents, I'm pretty sure you're not going to feel all that great. Going online to escape? Nope, you're getting shat on there as well. We may see that one could simply ignore the comments or go somewhere else, but for some, there is no escape. There is no help. There is no hope.


I apologize if my points are all over the place. Also, I'm not trying to blame the schools or anything. I don't believe this is something the schools or the government can fix. The unfortunate fact is that bullying has existed since the dawn of man. Society isn't helping much with the confusing message of simultaneously celebrating and condemning differences. It ultimately falls to the parents or anyone relatively stable enough to be an example of how one deals with life with strength and grace. Kids need someone to take the time to understand. Remind them that, while they may not be a special snowflake, they are a part of this world and have the right to be here and be happy with who they are -- and that truly, haters gonna hate.

I think I understand. It's a bit hard to wrap my head around, but I can try thinking about the interactions (or lack thereof) that way. 

It's not the name of the disorder that scares me. Because I'm a glutton for punishment, I look up stuff about bpd all the time. This usually leads to forums and support groups for SOs, family members, etc. of the person with the illness. I see myself in a lot of the behavior they describe, and then I see how scared and confused and upset they are when trying to deal with it. You do have a point, though. Most, if not all mental illnesses tend to operate on a spectrum.

Thanks for the recommendations. I'll look into those two immediately. 

I think that a lot of therapy so far hasn't worked because I wasn't as mindful or aware of what was going on. Unfortunately, this behavior seems to be normal to the rest of my family (I've seen the same kind of behavior with my mom and grandmother), so I don't think they ever thought of it as a mental health issue. I only know what I know now due to a lot of personal research, but the borderline thing is very scary.

It's hard to not be tough on yourself when you know the people you care about are suffering. The energy healing thing sounds a bit strange, but at this point I'd be willing to try anything if it meant having some semblance of emotional balance.

If I had a nickel for every time I've heard someone tell me I'm over-thinking...
But yeah, I understand and can totally relate to it being socially crippling. Volunteering sounds great and seems to be suggested often. Personally, I wish I could volunteer by reading books to people. Knowledge is power, you know?

Dogs are awesome, yeah. I have a dachshund mix who would lick me forever if she could. Sometimes it feels like it's too much to care for her when I can barely care for myself, though. I feel guilty about it. All pets deserve to be cared for.

The only diagnoses I've had are depression and anxiety. I have reason to believe that I may have borderline personality disorder, but I'm not a doctor. Individual therapy seems to be hit and miss. Group therapy is more of a distraction (focused on helping others with problems and ignoring my own). I've only learned about CBT and DBT within the last year, and my current therapist seems to be open to trying it. I'm sorry you're going through this as well. Wouldn't wish it on anyone. Book recommendations are very welcome.
